abstract: Biological invasions restructure ecological communities by bringing previously isolated organisms into contact, but the viral flow within the trophic network and its consequences have not been established. Here, we show viral exchange following the introduction of a parasitoid wasp released for classical biological control in citrus. Within a few years, viruses spread bidirectionally between native and exotic host-parasitoid trophic chains and reached a generalist hyperparasitoid at the fourth trophic level. Cohabitation and multiparasitism, two ubiquitous interactions between the two trophic chains, were sufficient for viruses to be transferred between species and maintained transgenerationally. A virus acquired by the introduced parasitoid increased its offspring production by 30%. Our results identify cryptic viruses as an overlooked dimension of biological invasions, reshaping trophic networks and the outcome of the species we deliberately introduce.
